summary: LIVE pipeline end-to-end test: three source-attributed non-US/global taxa, four registry-identified molecular entities, four cultural-use claims and all four biological domains per plant. Intentionally bounded validation batch, not the 30-organism hourly research quota.

organisms.geographic_context: Cultivated widely across West Africa, Northeast Africa, Caribbean and South and Southeast Asia; origin debated
local_names: bissap (Senegal and parts of West Africa)
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Edible calyces for beverages; the referenced analytical study also examines flowers. Calyx teas, standardized extracts and isolated anthocyanins are not interchangeable.
organisms.evidence_summary: Some human trials investigate blood pressure with varying preparations and limitations; phytochemical identity supported by chromatography and NMR.

organisms.geographic_context: Northeastern China, Russian Far East and Korean Peninsula; related S. sphenanthera must not be conflated
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Dried ripe fruit is the traditional medicinal material. Berry preparations and isolated lignans differ; confirm species before transferring chemical results.
organisms.evidence_summary: Lignan chemistry well studied; many biological effects based on animal and cellular work; interactions with CYP3A/P-glycoprotein possible.

organisms.geographic_context: Indian subcontinent and South/Southeast Asia; traditional use reported in Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Tibetan contexts
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Dried fruit used in documented traditions; primary chemical assay cited here isolated phenolics from galls rather than the same fruit preparation.
organisms.evidence_summary: Hydrolyzable tannins characterized; much therapeutic mechanistic research is preclinical, not proof of broad clinical efficacy.

compounds.evidence_summary: Major pigment isolated from Hibiscus sabdariffa floral material; chemical pigment identity does not establish human treatment efficacy.
Schisandra lignan; CYP/drug-interaction and cellular signaling research must not be mistaken for demonstrated clinical effects.
Phenolic isolated from Terminalia chebula galls; antioxidant assays do not demonstrate human antioxidant treatment outcomes.
Phenolic from Terminalia chebula; direct studies needed for human efficacy and safety.

occurrences.part: flowers (study); calyx composition must be considered by preparation

cultural_uses.preparation: water-based beverage with regional flavoring variations, described rather than instructed
cultural_uses.reported_use: Widely consumed as tart, colored beverage; this record is culinary heritage, not a claim of hypertension cure.
cultural_uses.limitations: Names and practices vary among regions and households.

cultural_uses.preparation: tart drink, often spiced; no prescriptive medicinal directions
cultural_uses.reported_use: Beverage traditions sustained through African diasporic communities and Caribbean festivals.
cultural_uses.limitations: A historical article is not a clinical efficacy or all-community ethnography source.

cultural_uses.region: China, including historical references to Korean Peninsula
cultural_uses.tradition: Traditional Chinese materia medica; publicly reported use
cultural_uses.preparation: traditionally dried-fruit herbal preparations; no formulation instructions
cultural_uses.reported_use: Traditional sources report use in cough, palpitations and sleep complaints; medicinal claims are historical, not validated clinical treatment outcomes.
cultural_uses.limitations: Similar S. sphenanthera has different chemical composition; label by species.

cultural_uses.tradition: Ayurveda, Siddha and related documented traditions
cultural_uses.preparation: traditional fruit-based herbal preparation; descriptive only
cultural_uses.reported_use: Traditionally described in digestive and general tonic contexts, sometimes within multi-herb systems.
cultural_uses.limitations: Historical use does not prove safety or efficacy; chemical assay cited elsewhere used galls rather than fruits.

domain_notes.text: Anthocyanins undergo metabolism, but no proven energy or ATP benefit from consuming hibiscus.
Some human trials report blood-pressure effects of hibiscus preparations; clinical heterogeneity and medication interactions limit interpretation.
No well-established benefit for cognition; antioxidant laboratory activity cannot be translated directly to improved memory.
Enjoyment and cultural significance of beverage are distinct from evidence for antidepressant or anxiolytic effects.
Lignan metabolic signaling explored experimentally; human energy or longevity improvements not established.
Lignan effects on CYP3A/P-glycoprotein raise medication interaction concerns; protective effects remain preparation- and evidence-specific.
Preclinical neural signaling findings exist, but no broadly established human cognitive improvement.
Traditional sleep-related uses are historically reported but clinical antidepressant or sleep efficacy is not established.
Phenolic anti-oxidative assay activity does not prove cellular energy benefits in people.
Extracts and isolated tannins show in vitro bioactivity; historical digestive use does not establish a treatment outcome.
No high-confidence evidence of human cognitive improvement.

safety.alert: Possible additional blood-pressure lowering with antihypertensive drugs; concentrated preparations differ from beverages. Pregnancy and long-term concentrated-extract safety not established.
Potential CYP3A and P-glycoprotein interactions with medications; similar Schisandra species should not be assumed interchangeable. Human dose and safety of isolated lignans remain uncertain.
Polyphenol and tannin content is variable; gastrointestinal effects and drug interactions are incompletely studied. Laboratory antimicrobial assays are not evidence that ingestion treats infections.
